title: Family & people
goal: Talk about your family, say whose something is, and use masculine, feminine and neuter nouns correctly.
intro: Gujarati family vocabulary is precise: there are different words for your father's brother (કાકા) and your mother's brother (મામા), your father's sister (ફોઈ) and your mother's sister (માસી). In this unit you will also meet Gujarati's **three genders** and the possessive endings -નો / -ની / -નું.

grammar.title: Three genders and their plurals
grammar.body:
Every Gujarati noun is **masculine, feminine or neuter**. The endings often tell you which:

**-ઓ -o → masculine**: છોકરો 'boy', દીકરો 'son'. Plural changes -o to -ā: છોકરા 'boys'.
**-ઈ -ī → usually feminine**: છોકરી 'girl'. Plural adds -ઓ: છોકરીઓ.
**-ઉં -uṃ → neuter**: છોકરું 'child'. Plural changes -uṃ to -āṃ: છોકરાં.

Nouns ending in a consonant must be learned: ઘર 'house' (n), વાત 'talk' (f), દેશ 'country' (m). Their plural often just adds **-ઓ**: ઘરો, વાતો. The plural -ઓ can also be added to the forms above (છોકરાઓ, છોકરાંઓ) — very common in speech.

Neuter is used for young children, for many objects, and for groups of mixed gender: છોકરાં can mean 'children' or 'kids of both sexes'.

grammar.title: Possession: -નો / -ની / -નું
grammar.body:
Gujarati marks the owner with a suffix meaning 'of' that **agrees with the thing owned** — like an adjective:

**-નો** *-no* before a masculine noun: રામનો ભાઈ 'Ram's brother'
**-ની** *-nī* before a feminine noun: રામની બહેન 'Ram's sister'
**-નું** *-nuṃ* before a neuter noun: રામનું ઘર 'Ram's house'
**-ના** *-nā* before masculine plurals (or respected persons): રામના પપ્પા
**-નાં** *-nāṃ* before neuter plurals: રામનાં છોકરાં

Pronouns have their own forms that agree the same way: મારો / મારી / મારું 'my', તમારો / તમારી / તમારું 'your'. Note respect plural: you say **મારા પપ્પા**, **મારા કાકા** (plural form) for respected male elders.

grammar.title: 'I have': મારે … છે
grammar.body:
Gujarati has no verb 'to have'. For family members and relationships, use the form **મારે** *māre* ('for me') + noun + **છે**. For things you carry, use **મારી પાસે** *mārī pāse* 'with me' (Unit 6).

મારે, તારે, તમારે, અમારે, આપણે, એને — 'I have, you have, …'.

dialogue.title: Looking at photos
dialogue.setting: Meera shows her friend Anjali a family photo on her phone.

lines.speaker: Meera
lines.native: આ મારા પપ્પા છે, અને આ મારી મમ્મી.
lines.roman: ā mārā pappā chhe, ane ā mārī mammī.
lines.en: This is my dad, and this is my mum.

lines.speaker: Meera
lines.native: એ મારો નાનો ભાઈ છે, કુણાલ.
lines.roman: e māro nāno bhāī chhe, Kuṇāl.

lines.speaker: Anjali
lines.en: Do you have a sister too?

lines.speaker: Meera
lines.native: હા, મોટી બહેન છે. એ લંડનમાં રહે છે.
lines.roman: hā, moṭī bahen chhe. e Landanmāṃ rahe chhe.
lines.en: Yes, an elder sister. She lives in London.

lines.speaker: Meera
lines.native: હા, મારાં દાદી. બધાં એમને બા કહે છે.
lines.roman: hā, mārāṃ dādī. badhāṃ emne bā kahe chhe.
lines.en: Yes, my grandmother. Everyone calls her Ba.
lines.note: respect plural મારાં for a female elder

culture: Family terms are used far beyond the family: a shopkeeper is *bhāī* or *kākā*, an older woman *ben* or *māsī*, and a friend's parents *kākā* and *kākī* (or *uncle* and *aunty*). Respected elders take plural verb and possessive forms — **મારા પપ્પા આવ્યા** 'my father came', not *āvyo*. In many Gujarati families grandmother is simply **બા** and grandfather **બાપુજી** or **દાદા**.
